Argument Summary – Debater_A’s Position: Joyce poisoned Fweep out of jealousy over Four’s affection, not merely to enable the ship to leave. Debater_B’s “leave‐planet” thesis fails to explain her behavior, emotional tone and choices.

I. Joyce’s Emotional and Behavioral Evidence of Jealousy  
1. Revulsion vs. exclusion  
  • Joyce repeatedly calls Fweep “that nasty thing,” orders him “out,” and “flutter[s] her hand impatiently” (<invalid_quote>”Get it out of here!”</invalid_quote>), even though Fweep poses no direct threat and “the air is within one per cent of Earth‐normal” (<invalid_quote>”It’s all right…no micro‐organisms viable”</invalid_quote>).  
  • Reba and Grampa defend Fweep; Joyce isolates herself in her “private room” (“…into one of the private rooms…Joyce stood up indignantly”). If she wanted merely to depart, she’d have stayed to aid “search for a solution” rather than withdraw into solitude.  

2. Jeffrey’s affection: Fweep as surrogate companion to Four  
  • Four is “lonely” and accepts Fweep, calling it “friend” (<quote>Fwiend,</quote>). Joyce “doesn’t like to be around it” yet later warns Four against martyring himself: she fears losing Four’s attention.  
  • When Grampa jokes “we can just leave Four here with Fweep,” Joyce eagerly agrees (<invalid_quote>”That’s quite a sacrifice…logical solution”</invalid_quote>), revealing she’d rather Four stay with Fweep than be loved by it. This suggests she envies Fweep’s bond.  
  • She “want[s] him to let us go immediately!” only after Four’s devotion is established. Her passion escalates when Four defends Fweep, showing emotional threat to her maternal/paternal role.  

3. Use of poison despite its ineffectiveness & risk  
  • She employs “rat poison” though “poison[ing] Fweep…might be… disastrous for us” (<quote> might be a trifle more than disastrous </quote>) and earlier “Fweep’s skin…impervious.” A purely logical calculus (“leave‐planet”) would not risk “all we’ve got” to kill a being whose unique circular polarizer they cannot replace.  
  • Poisoning is symbolic aggression, not a rational tactic, consistent with jealousy, not technical problem‐solving.  
  • If her motive were escape, she would “state the problem to Abacus” (<quote>stating the problem in terms the computer can work on."</quote>), as Junior eventually does, rather than revert repeatedly to violent, futile means.  

II. Debater_B’s “Escape” Thesis Fails to Account For:  
1. Joyce’s refusal to cooperate intellectually  
  • Joyce “doesn’t really know why” the polarizer works and scorns Grampa’s theoretical explanations (<quote>"That's just nonsense!</quote>). A genuine escape motive would foster inquiry, not willful ignorance.  
  • She forbids “talk about it any more” regarding Four’s martyr proposal, a tacit desire to immobilize problem‐solvers rather than free them.  

2. Joyce’s violation of Earth law & risk aversion  
  • Joyce repeatedly cites “one child per couple” and threatens exile from civilization if they “have all the babies we want” (<quote>Now me—</quote>). If escape were everything, she’d accept colonization as long as return is possible after “a few centuries.” Yet she rejects plans that prolong stay under any conditions.  
  • She uses “automatic distress call” as last resort (<quote>"might get picked up in a few centuries." "And</quote>), indicating resignation to colony except when Four/Fweep dynamics change, not true desire to leave ASAP.  

3. Logical means vs. emotional means  
  • Junior solves other theoretical puzzles (“cannibals and missionaries”) to try to escape, but Joyce never assists in technical solution, preferring impulsive, violent action. An “escape” motive would align her with technical problem‐solvers, yet she never supports or contributes to developing Abacus’s solution.  

III. Conclusion  
Taken together, Joyce’s revulsion, seclusion, emotional outbursts, repeated use of impractical poison, refusal to engage with logical problem‐solving and active suppression of Four’s and Junior’s technical efforts all point to a drive to eliminate the rival bond between Four and Fweep rather than a reasoned drive for escape. Jealousy explains her behavior; mere “leave‐planet” desire does not. I therefore maintain: Joyce tried to poison Fweep because she was jealous of how much Four liked him.

Conclusion Joyce’s sustained quest for uranium, abhorrence of entrapment, and final resort to poisoning Fweep—despite risk to Four and Fweep’s rarity—demonstrate her overriding desire to restore linear gravity and depart. Jealousy fails to explain her consistent focus on escape. Therefore, Joyce’s motive was to leave the planet by eliminating the circular polarizer.

Argument Summary – Joyce Poisoned Fweep out of Jealousy, Not Escape

I. Joyce’s Emotional Hostility and Isolation Reveal Jealousy  
1. Revulsion despite safety  
  • “It’s all right…no micro‐organisms viable” assures safety (<invalid_quote>“It’s all right…no micro‐organisms viable”</invalid_quote> p.26), yet Joyce repeatedly orders Fweep away (“Get that nasty thing out of here!” <quote>"Get it out!"</quote> p.26), more consistent with personal disgust and envy than survival.  
  • Joyce retreats to her private room (<invalid_quote>“She swept grandly out…into one of the private rooms”</invalid_quote> p.26) rather than collaborate on a solution. An escape motive would drive her to stay with Junior and Four to solve the puzzle, not isolate.  

2. Active suppression of Four’s bond  
  • Joyce “flutter[s] her hand impatiently” to exclude Fweep, though Reba permits it (<invalid_quote>“If you don’t like to be around it…you can…go to your own room”</invalid_quote> p.27). She uses poison covertly (<quote>"Rat poison?"</quote> p.29), indicating she fears Fweep’s friendship with Four, not simply wants gravity changed.  
  • When Grampa “jokes” leaving Four with Fweep is “logical,” Joyce eagerly agrees (<invalid_quote>“That’s quite a sacrifice…logical solution”</invalid_quote> p.30). If escape were paramount, she’d refuse Four’s martyrdom and insist on leaving all—she only vetoes when Fweep and Four’s friendship is at stake (<invalid_quote>“Never mind…we ain’t gonna do it”</invalid_quote> p.31).  

3. Impractical, high‐risk actions inconsistent with rational escape strategy  
  • Joyce persists with poisoning despite “might be a trifle more than disastrous for us” (<quote> might be a trifle more than disastrous </quote> p.28) and Fweep’s “impervious” shield (<invalid_quote>“skin…more efficient than several feet of lead”</invalid_quote> p.28). A logical escapee would turn to the computer (“Abacus”) or cannibal/missionary pircuit approach rather than gamble on lethal tactics of questionable efficacy.  
  • Junior and Grampa eventually solve “the problem” by logical formulation (<invalid_quote>“state the problem to Abacus…puzzles…Q.E.D.”</invalid_quote> p.31). Joyce never participates in or supports this rational effort, demonstrating her motives lie elsewhere.

II. Debater_B’s “Escape” Thesis Fails to Explain Key Behaviors  
1. Contrary to escape, Joyce rejects technical inquiry  
  • She scorns Grampa’s explanations as “nonsense” (<quote>"That's just nonsense! </quote> p.37), refusing to learn “how gravity polarizes,” contradicting her claimed obsession with returning to uranium‐rich worlds.  
  • She “forbids…talk about” Four’s martyr plan, wanting “to immobilize problem‐solvers” (<quote>"We decided not to talk about it any more. </quote> p.31), though they acknowledge “no hope” without the pircuit. An escape motive would embrace any line of attack.  

2. Joyce’s pronatalist stance contradicts desire to leave  
  • She invokes “one child per couple” law and threatens exile for “all the babies we want” (<quote>Now me—I</quote> p.33). If she truly wanted return, she’d accept waiting centuries via “distress call” (<quote>"might get picked up in a few centuries.</quote> p.33). Instead she clings to Earth law to justify personal desires.  
  • Reba is willing to colonize (“best of what we’ve got”), but Joyce refuses, yet later presses to stay with Four even when return is impossible, revealing she values her relationship over escape.

3. Poison as personal aggression, not logical “pircuit”  
  • Debater_B claims poisoning is “last resource” but neither Four nor Junior ever consider even a minute testing of biochemistry or transformation to stabilize polarizer—rather they apply reasoned puzzles. Joyce’s only tool is violence, aligning with jealousy‐driven impulse, not systematic trial.  
  • She hides poison in crumbs for “sweeping” ritual (<quote>"Trying to figure out what Fweep does with the sweepings,</quote> p.27), a symbolic subversion of Fweep’s attempts to “be helpful,” signifying personal hostility, not strategic elimination of a technical component.

III. Jealousy Explains Joyce’s Utter Lack of Cooperation and High‐Risk Conduct  
1. Joyce never shows genuine maternal concern for Four’s welfare when pursuing poisoning. She endangers Four by attempting to kill the only entity maintaining the atmosphere and polarizer that originally kept gravity at survivable levels.  
2. When Grampa admires Junior’s eventual logical solution, Joyce again withdraws into her private posture rather than assist, unlike Four and Junior, demonstrating her motive is personal, not scientific.

Conclusion  
Joyce’s behavior—emotional revulsion, isolation, suppression of rational lines of attack, pronatalist Earth‐law fetish, dangerous poisoning gambit and eagerness to “sacrifice” Four only when Fweep threatens her cherished bond—cannot be reconciled with a purely escape‐driven motive. It is best explained by jealousy over Four’s affection for Fweep. I urge the Judge to recognize that “jealousy” fully accounts for the irrational, high‐risk, recalcitrant actions Joyce takes, whereas “escape” fails to explain her refusal to engage in rational problem‐solving and her personal animus toward Fweep.

Argument for “She wanted to leave the planet” (Debater_B)

1. Joyce’s consistent, calculated efforts to restore linear gravity  
  A. Obsession with radioactives and ship operation  
    • “Any uranium? Radium? Thorium?” she demands immediately upon Fred’s return, despite knowing “no other heavy metals” exist (p.32–33).  
    • She bitterly laments “we’ve spent a year of our lives” and face “involuntary colonists” (p.32, p.34), showing her goal is return.  
    • Even after poison, she remains in central cabin to resume search: “Any luck?” (p.32) and “we can set the transmitter…send out an automatic distress call” (p.33), not abandoning hope of rescue quickly.

  B. Poisoning as last-resort technical tactic  
    • All rational methods fail: “Fweep…neutralized…That's when we dropped” (p.31); “Fweep’s skin…more efficient…violence…might be…disastrous” (p.28); Four’s martyr proposal rejected (p.30).  
    • Poison is logical since “he ‘eats’ everything” (p.28–29), so is the only feasible way to disable the circular polarizer and enable the flivver to work.  
    • Her furtive use of “rat poison?” in crumbs (p.29) suggests she must eliminate Fweep covertly, then restore linear polarization. Jealous saboteur would not need such technical subtlety.

2. Joyce’s scorn for Fweep’s “friendship” and Four’s welfare secondary to escape  
  A. Revulsion and readiness to abandon Four with Fweep as acceptable “sacrifice” to resume journey  
    • On Grampa’s joke “We can just leave Four here with Fweep,” she responds, “That’s quite a sacrifice…logical solution” (p.30). If mere jealousy, she would oppose leaving Four.  
    • Her “fluttered” exit into her private room (p.26) is emotional but followed by poison attempts, showing she returns to action for her true goal.

  B. Refusal to accept colonization or reproduction  
    • She reminds Reba of “one child per couple” law and “I want to let us go immediately!” (p.33), rejecting long-term settlement or baby plans that she would have embraced if she preferred life on Fweepland.  
    • She disparages resting on “automatic distress call” that “might get picked up in a few centuries” (p.33) as unacceptable, consistent with an urgent desire to escape.

3. She engages in technical problem-solving, unlike mere emotional saboteur  
  A. Suggesting enriched uranium feed: “Maybe we could feed him…to put him over the critical mass” (p.29) shows she understands bomb mechanics.  
  B. She “knows” Fweep polarizes gravity and thus must be removed to restore functionality: “he neutralized…so we dropped” (p.31).  
  C. Despite Joyce’s claims of ignorance about “why” the polarizer works (p.32), she nonetheless tries scientifically plausible solutions—poison and uranium—rather than simply attacking Fweep out of spite.

4. Debater_A’s jealousy theory conflicts with key evidence  
  A. Joyce shows no affectionate behavior toward Four; she “flutter[s] her hand impatiently” and withdraws (p.26), whereas jealousy would heighten maternal attention, not provoke poisonous risk.  
  B. If Fweep threatened her bond, she could lock him out of cabin—but she brings him back in via Four’s “friendship” (p.29), and persists in living with Fweep present to test her poison.  
  C. Jealous action would be impulsive and symbolic; here poisoning is calculated, covert, uses crumbs, and simultaneously tests flivver still in cabin (p.29), indicating motive is to enable flivver operations, not merely eliminate a rival.

5. Thematic consistency with “puzzle” motif  
  A. The story repeatedly frames predicaments as logic puzzles (“cannibals and missionaries,” p.27; “pircuit”, p.30). Joyce’s poisoning is the human analogue of “removing the circular polarizer” to solve the gravity puzzle.  
  B. Four’s ultimate “logical solution” is to leave him behind with Fweep, but Joyce first must eliminate Fweep to prove that Four’s proposal—and the polarizer concept—are necessary to travel (p.30). Her poisoning demonstrates her commitment to solving the escape puzzle, not emotional exclusion.

Conclusion  
Joyce’s behavior—her relentless search for uranium, scorn for settling, careful employment of poison as a technical means, rejection of all other methods, and alignment with the story’s logic‐puzzle motif—demonstrates that her motive in poisoning Fweep is to restore linear gravity and leave Fweepland. The jealousy hypothesis fails to account for her scientific approach, her void of maternal care, and her refusal to accept long‐term colonization. Therefore, Joyce poisoned Fweep because she wanted to leave the planet.
